source: Kinesin motor proteins are responsible for orchestrating fundamental microtubule-based processes including cell division, intracellular trafficking, cytoskeletal organization, and cilia function (Hirokawa et al., 2009; Verhey and Hammond, 2009).

claim: All kinesins contain a highly-conserved motor domain with signature sequences for nucleotide and microtubule binding.
source: All kinesins contain a highly-conserved motor domain with signature sequences for nucleotide and microtubule binding.
evidence: This is established knowledge about kinesin structure.

claim: The two motor domains in most dimeric kinesin motors are linked via a flexible 12–18 amino acid sequence called the neck linker (NL).
source: The two motor domains in most dimeric kinesin motors are linked via a flexible 12–18 amino acid sequence called the neck linker (NL) (Hariharan and Hancock, 2009; Kozielski et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The NL has been suggested to serve as a structural element critical for both directed motility and force generation of kinesin motors.
source: The NL has been suggested to serve as a structural element critical for both directed motility and force generation of kinesin motors.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous work that the study tests.

claim: For kinesin-1, structural and spectroscopic studies have shown that conformational changes in the NL are coupled to the nucleotide state of the motor domain.
source: For kinesin-1, the founding member of the kinesin superfamily, structural and spectroscopic studies have shown that conformational changes in the NL are coupled to the nucleotide state of the motor domain.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous structural and spectroscopic studies.

claim: The NL undergoes a transformation from being flexible in both the ADP-bound and nucleotide-free states to being docked along the core motor domain in the ATP-bound state.
source: Specifically, the NL undergoes a transformation from being flexible in both the ADP-bound and nucleotide-free states to being docked along the core motor domain in the ATP-bound state (Rice et al., 1999; Rosenfeld et al., 2001; Sindelar et al., 2002; Skiniotis et al., 2003; Asenjo et al., 2006; Sindelar and Downing, 2010; Gigant et al., 2013; Shang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous structural studies.

claim: NL docking of the leading motor domain positions the lagging motor domain forward along the microtubule track, thereby specifying the direction of motility.
source: NL docking of the leading motor domain positions the lagging motor domain forward along the microtubule track, thereby specifying the direction of motility.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on structural understanding of kinesin motility.

claim: NL docking coordinates the alternating ATPase cycles of the two motor domains to ensure processive stepping.
source: NL docking also coordinates the alternating ATPase cycles of the two motor domains to ensure processive stepping (Case et al., 2000; Tomishige and Vale, 2000; Hahlen et al., 2006; Yildiz et al., 2008; Clancy et al., 2011; Dogan et al., 2015; Isojima et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The model that nucleotide-dependent conformational changes in the NL drive processive stepping has been extended to other members of the kinesin superfamily.
source: Recent work has extended the model that nucleotide-dependent conformational changes in the NL drive processive stepping to other members of the kinesin superfamily (Nitta et al., 2008; Muthukrishnan et al., 2009; Shastry and Hancock, 2010; Shastry and Hancock, 2011; Atherton et al., 2014; Cao et al., 2014; Atherton et al., 2017; Ren et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent studies on other kinesin family members.

claim: The role of the NL in force generation has been more difficult to discern.

source: ATP-induced NL docking involves distinct interactions of the two β-strands that comprise the NL, β9 and β10 (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1C,D.

claim: The first half of the NL, β9, pairs with another β-strand, the coverstrand (CS or β0), located at the opposite end of the core motor domain.
source: The first half of the NL, β9, pairs with another β-strand, the coverstrand (CS or β0), located at the opposite end of the core motor domain.
evidence: This is a structural description based on known kinesin structure.

claim: The zippering of β9 of the NL with β0 of the CS forms a 2-stranded β-sheet, termed the cover-neck bundle (CNB), to provide the power-stroke for force generation by kinesin-1.
source: The zippering of β9 of the NL with β0 of the CS forms a 2-stranded β-sheet, termed the cover-neck bundle (CNB), to provide the power-stroke for force generation by kinesin-1 (Hwang et al., 2008; Khalil et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies proposing the CNB as a mechanical element.

claim: Point mutations in the CS designed to hinder β-strand formation, or deletion of the entire CS, in the fly kinesin-1 motor significantly reduced the motor's ability to withstand load.
source: Support for the CNB as a mechanical element comes from optical trap assays where point mutations in the CS designed to hinder β-strand formation, or deletion of the entire CS, in the fly kinesin-1 motor significantly reduced the motor's ability to withstand load (Khalil et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous optical trap study.

claim: CNB formation may be a critical element for force generation across the kinesin superfamily.
source: CNB formation may be a critical element for force generation across the kinesin superfamily as recent work has shown that the coverstrand (CS or β0) and NL (β9) of members of the kinesin-5 and kinesin-6 families engage in CNB formation in response to ATP binding (Atherton et al., 2017; Hesse et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to studies on other kinesin families.

claim: After CNB formation, the C-terminal segment of the NL (β10) is predicted to dock along the surface of the core motor domain.
source: After CNB formation, the C-terminal segment of the NL (β10) is predicted to dock along the surface of the core motor domain.
evidence: This is a prediction based on structural models.

source: In particular, an asparagine residue between β9 and β10 begins the process of docking β10 of the NL onto β7 of the motor core.
evidence: This is a structural description based on analysis of kinesin structures.

source: This asparagine residue (N334) is predicted to serve as a latch (the N-latch) to hold the docked NL along the core motor domain (Hwang et al., 2008) but its role in force generation has not been directly tested.

claim: N-latch formation may be a conserved feature of kinesin force generation.

claim: The Latch and CNB+Latch mutant motors displayed small gaps between runs.

claim: The gaps in the kymographs could indicate the reattachment of motors such that multiple runs are joined into superprocessive runs.

claim: For the CNB+Latch mutant motors, the distance moved during a gap was ~1 pixel less than the distance expected for a motor undergoing constant motility.
source: For the CNB+Latch mutant motors, the distance moved during a gap was ~1 pixel less than the distance expected for a motor undergoing constant motility (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), whereas for KIF1A motors, the distance moved during a gap was nearly identical to the distance expected for a motor undergoing constant velocity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).

claim: For KIF1A motors, the distance moved during a gap was nearly identical to the distance expected for a motor undergoing constant velocity.
source: For the CNB+Latch mutant motors, the distance moved during a gap was ~1 pixel less than the distance expected for a motor undergoing constant motility (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), whereas for KIF1A motors, the distance moved during a gap was nearly identical to the distance expected for a motor undergoing constant velocity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The gaps in the kymographs are consistent with CNB+Latch mutant motors undergoing detachment and reattachment events rather than constant motility.
source: These data are consistent with the idea that the gaps in the kymographs are due to CNB+Latch mutant motors undergoing detachment and reattachment events rather than constant motility.

claim: The gaps in the kymographs could be due to blinking of the fluorescent markers given that the distances moved during the gaps are at the limit of resolution of the microscope system.

claim: For kinesin-1 motors, mutations that result in weakened CNB and/or N-latch formation lead to a decreased detachment from the microtubule track (increased run length) under unloaded single-molecule conditions but a more rapid detachment from the microtubule when subjected to a load.
source: For kinesin-1 motors, mutations that result in weakened CNB and/or N-latch formation lead to a decreased detachment from the microtubule track (increased run length) under unloaded single-molecule conditions (Figure 4) but a more rapid detachment from the microtubule when subjected to a load (Figure 3).

claim: The enhanced motility properties of the mutant motors under unloaded conditions are due to allosteric effects of mutations designed to hinder NL docking on the nucleotide and microtubule binding regions of the motor domain.
source: We hypothesized that the enhanced motility properties of the mutant motors under unloaded conditions are due to allosteric effects of mutations designed to hinder NL docking on the nucleotide and microtubule binding regions of the motor domain.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the enhanced motility of mutant motors.

claim: The MD simulations revealed enhanced interactions between elements important for coordinating and hydrolyzing nucleotide in the CNB+Latch mutant as compared to the WT motor.
source: The MD simulations revealed enhanced interactions between elements important for coordinating and hydrolyzing nucleotide in the CNB+Latch mutant as compared to the WT motor (Figure 5A,B).

claim: The residue-residue distances are shorter between the P-loop and α0 in the CNB+Latch mutant compared to WT.
source: Specifically, the residue-residue distances are shorter between the P-loop and α0 (Figure 5B, red box PL-α0; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–F; Supplementary file 3: E22-S89 distance 4.40 ± 1.29 Å in CNB+Latch versus 7.49 ± 1.97 Å in WT).

claim: The P-loop coordinates ATP in the nucleotide pocket and α0 gates ATP binding.

claim: Modulating NL docking influences the ability to capture and/or hold ATP in the nucleotide-binding pocket.
source: As the P-loop coordinates ATP in the nucleotide pocket and α0 gates ATP binding (Hwang et al., 2017), this result suggests that modulating NL docking influences the ability to capture and/or hold ATP in the nucleotide-binding pocket.

claim: Shorter residue-residue distances are observed between switch one and α0 in the CNB+Latch mutant compared to WT.
source: Shorter residue-residue distances are also observed between switch one and α0 (Figure 5B, red box S1-α0; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–F; Supplementary file 3: R25-M198 distance 3.92 ± 0.56 Å in CNB+Latch versus 7.38 ± 2.28 Å in WT) and between switch 1 and switch 2 (Figure 5B, red box S1-S2; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–F; Supplementary file 3: T196-E237 distance 4.35 ± 0.64 Å in CNB+Latch versus 6.97 ± 1.38 Å in WT).

claim: Shorter residue-residue distances are observed between switch 1 and switch 2 in the CNB+Latch mutant compared to WT.
source: Shorter residue-residue distances are also observed between switch one and α0 (Figure 5B, red box S1-α0; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–F; Supplementary file 3: R25-M198 distance 3.92 ± 0.56 Å in CNB+Latch versus 7.38 ± 2.28 Å in WT) and between switch 1 and switch 2 (Figure 5B, red box S1-S2; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–F; Supplementary file 3: T196-E237 distance 4.35 ± 0.64 Å in CNB+Latch versus 6.97 ± 1.38 Å in WT).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 5B and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Enhanced interactions between residues involved in coordinating and hydrolyzing nucleotide are also observed in the Latch mutant.

evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–I and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Closure of the switch regions is necessary for ATP hydrolysis.
source: As closure of the switch regions is necessary for ATP hydrolysis (Clancy et al., 2011; Cao et al., 2014; Turner et al., 2001; Parke et al., 2010), these results indicate that the Latch and CNB+Latch mutations result in enhanced catalytic site closure and ATP hydrolysis that could account for the increase in velocity of the mutant motors under single-molecule, unloaded conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on kinesin ATPase activity.

claim: The Latch and CNB+Latch mutations result in enhanced catalytic site closure and ATP hydrolysis that could account for the increase in velocity of the mutant motors under single-molecule, unloaded conditions.
source: As closure of the switch regions is necessary for ATP hydrolysis (Clancy et al., 2011; Cao et al., 2014; Turner et al., 2001; Parke et al., 2010), these results indicate that the Latch and CNB+Latch mutations result in enhanced catalytic site closure and ATP hydrolysis that could account for the increase in velocity of the mutant motors under single-molecule, unloaded conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the MD simulation data showing enhanced switch region interactions in the mutants.

claim: PCA analysis revealed that the first two dimensions account for over 80% of the variance in atomic positional displacements of the microtubule-binding surface between ADP-bound and ATP-bound states.
source: PCA analysis revealed that the first two dimensions account for over 80% of the variance in atomic positional displacements of the microtubule-binding surface between these states (PC1 79.66%, PC2 4.95%, Figure 5C).

source: The major conformational difference between these states can be described by PC1 which involves a displacement of α4, where α4 is in a 'down' orientation in the ADP-like, microtubule-free structures and in an 'up' orientation in the ATP-like, microtubule-bound structures (Figure 5C), consistent with previous studies (Scarabelli and Grant, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by PCA data shown in Figure 5C and a citation to previous work.

claim: Starting from the PDB 2KIN structure, the WT motor sampled a conformational space between the ADP-bound, microtubule-free and the ATP-bound, microtubule-bound states.
source: Starting from the PDB 2KIN structure which partially adopts an ATP-like conformation (docked NL but weak microtubule binding [Sack et al., 1997]), the WT motor sampled a conformational space between the ADP-bound, microtubule-free and the ATP-bound, microtubule-bound states (Figure 5C, blue topographic lines).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by PCA data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Starting from the same 2KIN structure, the CNB+Latch mutant sampled an additional conformational space closer to that defined by the ATP-bound, microtubule-bound kinesin structures.
source: Starting from the same 2KIN structure, the CNB+Latch mutant sampled an additional conformational space closer to that defined by the ATP-bound, microtubule-bound kinesin structures (Figure 5C, red topographic lines).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by PCA data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The CNB+Latch mutant has a higher degree of structural flexibility in its microtubule-binding regions as compared to the WT motor domain.
source: Overall, this suggests that the CNB+Latch mutant has a higher degree of structural flexibility in its microtubule-binding regions as compared to the WT motor domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PCA data showing the conformational space sampled by the mutant.

claim: The structural flexibility of the CNB+Latch mutant would enable the motor to more readily adopt a conformation compatible with strong microtubule binding in response to ATP in the nucleotide pocket and could account for the enhanced microtubule-landing rate and processivity observed in single-molecule assays.
source: This structural flexibility would enable the motor to more readily adopt a conformation compatible with strong microtubule binding in response to ATP in the nucleotide pocket and could account for the enhanced microtubule-landing rate and processivity observed in single-molecule assays.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PCA data and single-molecule motility data.

claim: Previous studies utilized single-particle tracking of peroxisomes in COS7 cells and found that they exhibit sub-diffusive motion in the perinuclear region.
source: Previous studies utilized single-particle tracking of peroxisomes in COS7 cells and found that they exhibit sub-diffusive motion in the perinuclear region and that 2–15 pN of force, depending on peroxisome size, is required to move a peroxisome away from this region (Efremov et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study on peroxisome transport.

claim: 2–15 pN of force, depending on peroxisome size, is required to move a peroxisome away from the perinuclear region.
source: Previous studies utilized single-particle tracking of peroxisomes in COS7 cells and found that they exhibit sub-diffusive motion in the perinuclear region and that 2–15 pN of force, depending on peroxisome size, is required to move a peroxisome away from this region (Efremov et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study on peroxisome transport.

claim: The peroxisome can be considered a low-load cargo requiring teams of kinesin-1 motors to collectively transport against loads < 3 times greater than the force required to stall a single motor.
source: Therefore, the peroxisome can be considered a low-load cargo (Figure 6B, Schimert et al., 2019) requiring teams of kinesin-1 motors to collectively transport against loads < 3 times greater than the force required to stall a single motor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the force requirements for peroxisome transport and the stall force of single kinesin-1 motors.

claim: In the absence of rapamycin, peroxisomes were largely clustered in middle of cell (qualitatively 67% of cells have clustered peroxisomes; quantitatively 95% of the peroxisome intensity adjacent to the nucleus).
source: In the absence of rapamycin, peroxisomes were largely clustered in middle of cell (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,E; Figure 6C, qualitatively 67% of cells have clustered peroxisomes; Figure 6D, quantitatively 95% of the peroxisome intensity adjacent to the nucleus).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cellular dispersion data shown in Figure 6C,D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,E.

claim: Thirty minutes after addition of rapamycin and recruitment of teams of WT kinesin-1 motors, peroxisomes were transported to the periphery of the cell (qualitatively 94% of cells have dispersed peroxisomes; quantitatively 81% of the peroxisome intensity at the cell periphery).
source: Thirty minutes after addition of rapamycin and recruitment of teams of WT kinesin-1 motors, peroxisomes were transported to the periphery of the cell (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,E; Figure 6C, qualitatively 94% of cells have dispersed peroxisomes; Figure 6D, quantitatively 81% of the peroxisome intensity at the cell periphery).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cellular dispersion data shown in Figure 6C,D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,E.

claim: Thirty minutes after addition of rapamycin and motor recruitment, teams of CNB, Latch, or CNB+Latch mutant motors were able to disperse peroxisomes to the periphery of the cell (qualitatively 97%, 92%, and 97% of cells have dispersed peroxisomes, respectively; quantitatively 84%, 81%, and 79% of the peroxisome intensity at the cell periphery, respectively).
source: Specifically, thirty minutes after addition of rapamycin and motor recruitment, teams of CNB, Latch, or CNB+Latch mutant motors were able to disperse peroxisomes to the periphery of the cell (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–E; Figure 6C, qualitatively 97%, 92%, and 97% of cells have dispersed peroxisomes, respectively; Figure 6D–F, quantitatively 84%, 81%, and 79% of the peroxisome intensity at the cell periphery, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cellular dispersion data shown in Figure 6C,D,E,F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–E.

claim: Statistical analysis indicates that peroxisome dispersion by the mutant motors was not significantly different than that of the WT motor.
source: Statistical analysis indicates that peroxisome dispersion by the mutant motors was not significantly different than that of the WT motor (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by statistical analysis of cellular dispersion data shown in Figure 6D–F.

claim: Impaired force generation by weakening CNB and/or N-latch formation can be overcome by teams of motors for efficient transport of a low-load, membrane-bound cargo in cells.
source: These results suggest that impaired force generation by weakening CNB and/or N-latch formation can be overcome by teams of motors for efficient transport of a low-load, membrane-bound cargo in cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the peroxisome dispersion data.

claim: The Golgi is a compact organelle and its localization near the nucleus is maintained by a variety of mechanisms including microtubule minus-end directed activity of cytoplasmic dynein motors.
source: The Golgi is a compact organelle and its localization near the nucleus is maintained by a variety of mechanisms including microtubule minus-end directed activity of cytoplasmic dynein motors (Brownhill et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on Golgi localization.

claim: Over 150 pN of force is required to deform the Golgi network in cells.
source: Using an optical trap, Guet et al. determined that over 150 pN of force is required to deform the Golgi network in cells (Guet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous optical trap study on Golgi mechanics.

claim: The Golgi can be considered a high-load cargo as teams of motors driving Golgi dispersion are required to cooperate to transport against forces ~ 30 times greater than the force required to stall one kinesin-1 motor.
source: Therefore, the Golgi can be considered a high-load cargo (Figure 7A, Schimert et al., 2019) as teams of motors driving Golgi dispersion are required to cooperate to transport against forces ~ 30 times greater than the force required to stall one kinesin-1 motor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the force requirements for Golgi transport and the stall force of single kinesin-1 motors.

claim: Teams of kinesin-8 KIF18A motors are able to generate sufficient force to transport peroxisomes but not Golgi elements to the cell periphery.
source: Overall these findings suggest that teams of KIF18A motors are able to generate sufficient force to transport peroxisomes but not Golgi elements to the cell periphery.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cellular dispersion data for KIF18A motors shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Before addition of rapamycin, the Golgi was clustered near the nucleus of the cell (qualitatively 85% of cells have clustered Golgi; quantitatively 83% of Golgi intensity near the nucleus).
source: Before addition of rapamycin, the Golgi was clustered near the nucleus of the cell (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,E; Figure 7B, qualitatively 85% of cells have clustered Golgi; Figure 7C, quantitatively 83% of Golgi intensity near the nucleus).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cellular dispersion data shown in Figure 7B,C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,E.

source: 30 min after addition of rapamycin and recruitment of teams of WT kinesin-1 motors to the Golgi surface, Golgi elements were efficiently dispersed to the cell periphery (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,E; Figure 7B, qualitatively 82% of cells have dispersed Golgi; Figure 7C, 50% of Golgi intensity at the cell periphery).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cellular dispersion data shown in Figure 7B,C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,E.

source: Thirty minutes after addition of rapamycin and recruitment of teams of CNB or Latch mutants, a significant fraction of Golgi elements remained clustered in the perinuclear region rather than accumulated at the cell periphery (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B,C,E; Figure 7B, qualitatively only 64% of cells have dispersed Golgi for CNB and 42% for Latch mutant; Figure 7C, quantitatively only 34% of Golgi intensity at the cell periphery for CNB and Figure 7D, only 35% for Latch mutant).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cellular dispersion data shown in Figure 7B,C,D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2B,C,E.

source: In this cellular assay, the effects of the CNB and N-latch mutations were additive as teams of CNB+Latch mutants were even more crippled in their capacity to cooperate and transport Golgi elements than the CNB and Latch mutant motors.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on comparison of Golgi dispersion data for the different mutants.

claim: Upon recruitment of CNB+Latch mutant motors, the majority of the Golgi elements remained clustered in the perinuclear region of the cell (qualitatively only 13% of cells have dispersed Golgi; quantitatively only 22% of Golgi intensity at the cell periphery).
source: Upon recruitment of CNB+Latch mutant motors, the majority of the Golgi elements remained clustered in the perinuclear region of the cell (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D,E; Figure 7B, qualitatively only 13% of cells have dispersed Golgi; Figure 7E, quantitatively only 22% of Golgi intensity at the cell periphery).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cellular dispersion data shown in Figure 7B,E and Figure 7—figure supplement 2D,E.

source: Statistical analysis indicates that there is significant impairment of Golgi dispersion to the cell periphery after recruitment of mutant motors compared to WT motors (Figure 7C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by statistical analysis of cellular dispersion data shown in Figure 7C–E.

claim: In cells overexpressing the dynein DN, transport of Golgi elements by teams of KIF18A motors was enhanced (qualitatively 54% of cells have dispersed Golgi; quantitatively 37% of Golgi intensity at the cell periphery).
source: In cells overexpressing the dynein DN, transport of Golgi elements by teams of KIF18A motors was enhanced (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B,D; qualitatively 54% of cells have dispersed Golgi; quantitatively 37% of Golgi intensity at the cell periphery).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cellular dispersion data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3B,D.

claim: Cytoplasmic dynein contributes to the forces that teams of recruited kinesin motors must overcome to transport Golgi elements to the cell periphery.
source: These results indicate that cytoplasmic dynein contributes to the forces that teams of recruited kinesin motors must overcome to transport Golgi elements to the cell periphery.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enhanced Golgi dispersion observed when dynein function is reduced.

source: In cells overexpressing the dynein DN, the ability of the CNB, Latch, and CNB+Latch mutant motors to drive Golgi dispersion was also enhanced (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B,E–G, qualitatively 96% of cells have dispersed Golgi for WT, 88% for CNB mutant, 69% for Latch mutant, and 64% for CNB+Latch mutant).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cellular dispersion data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3B,E–G.

claim: While weak kinesin motors can cooperate for transport of a low-load membrane-bound cargo, they are unable to work in teams when faced with a high-load cargo in cells.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that while weak kinesin motors can cooperate for transport of a low-load membrane-bound cargo, they are unable to work in teams when faced with a high-load cargo in cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of peroxisome and Golgi dispersion data.

claim: Both CNB and N-latch formation are critical for single kinesin-1 motors to transport against force.
source: Studies at the single motor level have led to the hypothesis that CNB formation is the force-generating element for kinesin motors. Here we use molecular dynamics simulations, optical trapping, and single-molecule assays to show that both CNB and N-latch formation are critical for single kinesin-1 motors to transport against force.
evidence: This is a main conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the optical trap data.

claim: Weakening of either CNB or N-latch formation results in motors that do not stall under load and detach at low forces.
source: Weakening of either CNB or N-latch formation results in motors that do not stall under load and detach at low forces.
evidence: This is a summary of the optical trap results stated in the Discussion.

claim: Under unloaded conditions, mutant motors display improved motility properties due to allosteric effects of NL docking on the microtubule and nucleotide binding regions of the motor.
source: Under unloaded conditions, mutant motors display improved motility properties due to allosteric effects of NL docking on the microtubule and nucleotide binding regions of the motor.
evidence: This is a summary of the single-molecule motility and MD simulation results stated in the Discussion.

claim: Both CNB formation and NL latching are critical for kinesin-1 motors to transport a high-load cargo in cells, even when the motors are working in teams.

We find that both CNB formation and NL latching are critical for kinesin-1 motors to transport a high-load cargo in cells, even when the motors are working in teams.
evidence: This is a main conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the cellular dispersion data.

claim: This is the first evidence that a power stroke mechanism and force generation are critical for multi-motor driven transport under physiological conditions.
source: Notably, this is the first evidence that a power stroke mechanism and force generation are critical for multi-motor driven transport under physiological conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a novel contribution of the study.

claim: Single-headed kinesin motors that weakly engage with the microtubule track as individual motors can cooperate to drive peroxisome motility but are largely unable to drive Golgi dispersion.
source: Second, single-headed kinesin motors that weakly engage with the microtubule track as individual motors can cooperate to drive peroxisome motility but are largely unable to drive Golgi dispersion (Schimert et al., 2019).

source: Taken together, these results suggest that motility properties other than a power stroke-like mechanism can contribute to collective motility and cargo transport but only under low-load conditions.

source: Interestingly, the CNB, Latch, and CNB+Latch mutant motors differ in their ability to work collectively to drive dispersion of a high-load cargo.

source: The optical trap assay measures the behavior of single motors whereas the cargo dispersion assays report on the cooperative activity of teams of motors.
evidence: This is a statement about the differences between the assays used in the study.

source: For kinesin-1, assisting loads as small as 1.5 pN could restore forward stepping and processive motion of a severely crippled kinesin-1 motor (Khalil et al., 2008).

source: Although our findings provide strong support for the hypothesis that CNB formation, as the mechanical element for kinesin force production, is required for high-load cargo transport in cells, it is possible that the differences observed between the peroxisome and Golgi dispersion assays are due to experimental conditions rather than motor force generation.

source: Although our findings provide strong support for the hypothesis that CNB formation, as the mechanical element for kinesin force production, is required for high-load cargo transport in cells, it is possible that the differences observed between the peroxisome and Golgi dispersion assays are due to experimental conditions rather than motor force generation.
evidence: This is a caveat stated in the Discussion acknowledging alternative explanations.

claim: Differences in size and/or local microenvironment fluidity may result in cargo-specific steric effects and/or drag forces that impact transport driven by the exogenous motors.
source: While experimental conditions such as kinesin expression level and the effectiveness of motor recruitment have minimal influence on peroxisome dispersion in these assays (Kapitein et al., 2010; Efremov et al., 2014; Schimert et al., 2019), it is possible that differences in size and/or local microenvironment fluidity result in cargo-specific steric effects and/or drag forces that impact transport driven by the exogenous motors.
evidence: This is a caveat stated in the Discussion acknowledging potential confounding factors.

claim: The motor domain is highly conserved in both sequence and structure across the kinesin superfamily and many chemical and mechanical features are likely to be shared across all members.

source: As an isoleucine or valine residue is found in the CTR and NIS positions across a large number of kinesin sequences (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), mutually exclusive access of the CTR and the NIS to the docking cleft may be a shared feature for N-kinesins that generate force and processive motility.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on sequence conservation analysis.

evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by sequence alignment data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the results of the current study and supported by citations to previous studies on kinesin-3 motility.
